note:
Vol. II No. 10, the last Democrat before the scene issue of 1 July, and the longest transcription in the range at 4,783 lines. Most of its length is the State Bank of Illinois charter and the commissioners' journal printed entire, which the editor apologises for.

PAGE 3 IS THE WORST-SEGMENTED COLUMN SET IN THE WHOLE RANGE. Its six 'columns' are strict line-by-line interleaves of two real ones — the federal land-sale proclamation woven through the advertising, one line each alternately — so the prices current arrives as a ladder of bare figures with township numbers between them and several advertisements survive only as every other line of themselves. Every claim off page 3 here therefore uses `lines_of_claim` to name its own alternate lines, and the prices current is read only where the reading is certain: the shredding is stated rather than worked around.

WHAT SURVIVES IS STILL WORTH IT: a THIRD named coffee house (the Eagle, Trowbridge's), a DENTIST on Lake Street, a new AUCTION AND COMMISSION house on South Water Street whose first sale falls on the scene date itself, a new boot and shoe manufactory on Lake Street, and flour at fifteen to sixteen dollars.

CHICAGO IS WELL ON THE EVE OF THE SCENE DATE, AND THE STATE AROUND IT IS NOT. 'Our own Town, Chicago, is uncommonly healthy' — printed 24 June 1835, in a column reporting cholera at Springfield, about twenty deaths in three weeks at Alton, and rumours at Galena and Ottawa.

WHY THIS IS THE CLAIM THAT SETTLES THE QUESTION. The 1835-05-20 and 1835-06-17 editorials describe streets and vacant lots so foul that the editor predicts pestilence, and it would be easy to model a sick town on the strength of them. This is the same editor, five weeks and one week later respectively, stating flatly that the town is UNCOMMONLY healthy while an epidemic runs elsewhere in Illinois — and staking his paper on publishing 'all the facts' if it changes. He is a hostile witness to his own sanitary campaign here, which is what makes the statement strong.

So the town on 1 July 1835: filthy, overcrowded, expensive, building fast, and not sick.

entities.role: Secretary of State of Illinois, who had not sent the town its charter

claims.notes:
THE THIRD AND ANGRIEST PRINTING OF THE MISSING CHARTER, one week before the scene date, and the one that names the man: Secretary Field, and the paper wants his office abolished. It adds one fact the earlier two do not — the CORPORATION ITSELF ordered a copy 'several months since', and so did several private citizens, and neither request was answered.

THE SETTLED POSITION AT THE SCENE DATE, from the three printings together (1835-05-20, 1835-06-10, this): an act enlarging the powers of the corporation of Chicago was passed in February 1835; no copy had reached the town by 24 June; the election of new Trustees under it was repeatedly adjourned for want of the text; and the town was accordingly still governed on 1 July 1835 by the Trustees elected under its 1833 charter — the 'present Trustees' the town meeting of 16 June asked to clean the streets.

FLOUR HAS TRIPLED IN A MONTH AND THE BUILDING MATERIALS HAVE NOT MOVED A CENT.

Superfine flour: $5.00-6.50 on 27 May, $10.00-12.00 on 4 and 10 June, $15.00-16.00 here, one week before the scene date. Fine flour is $13.00. Salt, Indian meal and buckwheat are unchanged from the first table. And every one of the seven building materials is IDENTICAL to its 27 May figure for the fourth consecutive week: lumber 28-29, shingles 3.00-3.50, square timber 5-6, brick 5-6, stone 6.00-6.50, lime .75-.88, wood 2.50.

THAT DIVERGENCE IS THE FINDING OF THE FOUR TABLES TOGETHER. A town whose bread price tripled in a month while its brick, lumber and lime prices did not twitch was not short of building supply — it was short of food, because people were arriving faster than provisions. The 4 June editorial says exactly that in words ('The increase of consumption has been so rapid in Chicago, that our stock of eatables is almost exhausted') and the 17 June one supplies the crowd. Three independent readings, one conclusion.

THIS TABLE IS READ PARTIALLY AND ON PURPOSE. Page 3 of this issue interleaves the prices current with the federal land-sale proclamation LINE BY LINE, so the table arrives as single figures separated by township numbers. Only the rows whose label and figures both survive in the alternation are read — the head, salt, the two flours, buckwheat, Indian meal, and the whole building-materials block, which happens to fall in a clean run. THE PROVISIONS AND GRAIN ROWS ARE NOT READ: their figures are present as bare numbers (lines 2342-2400) and assigning them to rows would be reconstruction from the previous weeks' table, not reading, and the whole point of quoting four tables is to see what moved. Where a row is not read it is simply absent from the normalized reading.

claims.notes:
THE CLAIM THAT PUTS THE EAGLE COFFEE HOUSE IN DEARBORN STREET — and it does so through a hole. The advertisement survives only as every other line of itself, and the two lines that matter read 'aq Harmon. in Dearborn street,' and 'of the "Eaglo Coffee House."' with an unrecoverable line between them. So the office is in Dearborn Street, it involves somebody named Harmon, and it stands in some stated relation to the Eagle Coffee House — and THE PREPOSITION IS GONE. 'opposite the', 'a few doors from the', 'nearly opposite the' and 'in the rear of the' all fit the surviving fragment and this pass will not choose between them.

WHAT IS THEREFORE ASSERTED AND WHAT IS NOT. Asserted: Abell's office is in Dearborn Street; the Eagle Coffee House is named in the same address and is therefore in or about Dearborn Street. NOT asserted: which side, how far, or whether the Eagle is ON Dearborn at all rather than merely visible from the office. The placement class is `relative` because that is the shape of the statement, and the offset text is quoted with its gap showing.

'Harmon' is very likely the Harmon of Harmon, Loomis & Co. — but that firm states its own store to be in SOUTH WATER street, and this line says Dearborn, so the identification would create the same conflict Magie & Wilkinson already carry. Not merged. The lawyer's forename is not printed in the surviving lines and is not supplied; a 'Goodrich & Abell' appears in the 31 March letter list and may be the same man, which is T-0304's kind of question.

A NEW AUCTION AND COMMISSION HOUSE OPENS ON SOUTH WATER STREET AND ITS FIRST SALE IS ON THE SCENE DATE. 'His first public sale will take place on Wednesday next, the 1st day of July' — 1 July 1835 was a Wednesday, and this is the only event in the entire corpus advertised to happen ON the modelled day, at a named street, in a taken-over store. Goods were to be delivered to the store before the 1st, so on the morning of the scene date that building held a stock waiting to be sold and a crowd was expected in it.

Cohen's Store' since December 1833 and Cohen is on South Water Street, so a bootmaker turning auctioneer on the same street is possible and so is a second Montgomery. claims.notes:
A MARRIAGE IN CHICAGO ON 20 JUNE 1835, ELEVEN DAYS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, AND THE NOTICE IS HALF DESTROYED. The interleave has taken every other line, so what survives is the dateline, three names and the fact that one of them is 'Esq. Merchant of this town'. WHO MARRIED WHOM CANNOT BE READ — there appear to be two marriages in the paragraph rather than one (a Dupage Settlement Hubbard, a Peck of this town, and a Willis of Philadelphia), and pairing them would be invention.

WHAT IS MINTED IS THE THREE NAMES AND NOTHING ELSE: no spouse, no relationship, no officiant. PECK, ESQ., MERCHANT OF THIS TOWN is the useful one — a Peck addressed the town meeting of 16 June and sat on its committee of seven, and this supplies his trade. The two readings are not merged on that alone, but the occupation is recorded where a later pass can use it.
